props.title: Run, Man, Run
props.initialSlug: Mexican gunslinger seeks fortune in violent frontier

sections.content: Run, Man, Run stands as Sergio Sollima's explosive finale to his political western trilogy, following The Big Gundown (1966) and Face to Face (1967). This often-overlooked Zapata Western stars Tomas Milian as Cuchillo, the knife-throwing peasant first introduced in The Big Gundown, now caught up in a revolutionary plot involving hidden Mexican gold. Unlike typical Spaghetti Westerns focused purely on revenge or greed, Sollima infuses sharp political commentary about class struggle and revolution, setting it apart from contemporaries like The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (1966).

sections.content: Ennio Morricone's score for Run, Man, Run deserves special attention, marking one of his most dynamic and experimental western soundtracks. The main theme's driving percussion and urgent vocals perfectly capture Cuchillo's desperate flight, while incorporating Mexican folk elements that ground the film in its revolutionary setting. This approach influenced later politically-conscious westerns like Duck, You Sucker (1971) and A Bullet for the General (1966). SUBHEAD: Political Western Evolution

Run, Man, Run represents the peak of the Zapata Western subgenre, which emerged from Italian filmmakers' interest in Mexican revolutionary themes. Unlike the straightforward morality of American westerns like The Magnificent Seven (1960), these films presented complex views of revolution and social justice. Sollima's trilogy, particularly Run, Man, Run, influenced later revisionist westerns like The Professional (1966) and Companeros (1970) with its ambiguous treatment of heroism and political idealism.
